spec: Which files at a firmware destination are the DISTRIBUTION's own copy rather than something a user placed. World knowledge under DESIGN.md's boundary rule, and of the narrowest possible kind: the table states only WHICH trees and files one COMPONENT's preparation step copies into the firmware root — for RetroDECK the RetroArch component's, which is where that root's own trees come from — read line by line out of the shipped script, while whether the file at a destination really is that copy is decided on the machine: the shipped file and the placed file are hashed and the statement is made only when they are equal. Other components write into the same root by other means (see ROADMAP section 6), so this list is not a census of everything a distribution puts there. Nothing here is a claim about any particular machine. A distribution is keyed by the arrangement kind atlas already answers under ('retrodeck'), so the word in the contract and the word a handle reports are one word. 'source' is relative to 'source_root', which is spelled the way the DISTRIBUTION spells it — inside its Flatpak sandbox — because that is the path its own script names; the resolver translates it to a host path through the same sandbox map the save and firmware routes translate configured values with. 'kind' says WHAT the copy places: 'tree' (a whole directory, so every file below the destination has a counterpart below the source) or 'file' (one file, matched exactly). It is not read off the cp flag — RetroDECK copies both trees and files with cp -rf and uses cp -f on one line only — and it is not derived from the source's spelling either, because directory names like 'qemu' and 'fbneo' carry no extension to derive from. Destinations and sources may differ — RetroDECK's MSX and Amiga trees are renamed on the way — so the renaming is recorded rather than assumed away. The version pin is provenance, NOT a gate: unlike content_tree_wiring.json, whose promise can only be measured against the version that made it, every statement this table supports rests on a hash equality read from the live machine, so a table that has fallen behind a release under-reports and the equality behind a statement it does make was still measured. The one thing a stale entry can still get wrong is the REPAIR it implies: if a release stops copying a tree while going on shipping it, the bytes still match and 'the component prepare puts this back' no longer holds — which is a reason to re-read the script at a release, not to gate the answer. A destination that no entry covers, and a file whose bytes differ from the shipped one, are both simply not stated.
